newsitem.title: PERU: FEATURE-Lima proudly displays its "monumental" mistakes.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Lima proudly displays its "monumental" mistakes.

text.p: A sculptor who commited suicide after realising an error in his work, a strange animal on a statue of the motherland, even a statue that "stood up" are a few of the bizarre tales hidden behind Lima's monuments.

Although almost six million people move daily through the squares, streets and parks of this sprawling colonial city, few are aware of the myriad errors and curiosities hidden behind the hundreds of monuments erected here over the centuries. Across from the colonial balconies and pastel-coloured buildings in San Martin Square, for example, an Andean llama goes almost unnoticed between laurels in the head of a sculpture of the Madre Patria (Mother Country).
"It has a long snout and tall ears ... It looks to me a little bit more like a bat", said passerby Edwin Garcilaso, 19, laconically contemplating the misplaced llama.

"It looks like it was a error of interpretation," wrote the late author Ernesto Ascher in his book "Curiosities of Lima," a compendium of odd stories about Peru's coastal capital. Ascher explained that Spanish sculptor Mariano Benlluire had ordered his helper to put a torch light, also called "llama" in Spanish, on top of the sculpture, but the helper got confused and put the animal there instead.

A few blocks away, in the middle of Lima's chaotic traffic and under the dense clouds that cover it for most of the year, stands the monument to Miguel Grau, a hero of a 19th century war that Peru fought against neighbouring Chile. On the back of the monument there is an engraving of the Peruvian warship Huascar cruising from left to right in rough seas, while the smoke coming from the ship that Grau commanded defies the laws of nature and also goes from left to right.

"Impossible. I cannot believe this," proclaimed a bemused Lima taxi driver as he raised his voice over the noises of the city and swerved around the potholes beside Grau's monument. To add to the incongruity, Grau's cape, sword and boots do not belong to a navy commander but a cavalry officer.

In other cases, the mistakes have had serious consequences like the death of Italian sculptor Adamo Tadolini, who took his own life after someone pointed out an error in his monument of Latin American "Liberator" Simon Bolivar located near Congress. Tadolini did the representation of Bolivar riding a charger. The work, inaugurated on Dec. 9, 1859, received much praise until someone realised that a crucial part of the harness was missing.
"It is said that Tadolini suffered such shock with the observation that, taking out his pistol, he shot himself in the temple, dying at the feet of his masterpiece," Ascher wrote.

But there are not only mistakes in the bizarre litany of tales surrounding the monuments of Lima, whose streets perch on the edge of the Pacific where the Andean mountains tumble down onto a narrow desert strip and then into the sea.

Other monuments have earned notoriety for their strange behaviour, like the sculpture of an ex-president that "stood up" after its inauguration and another that somehow managed to inaugurate itself, the author's son, Ernesto Ascher Jr, told Reuters. He said the first monument to ex-President Manuel Candamo represented him seated quietly until one morning an explosion destroyed the entire sculpture except for the legs.

Several years after the explosion, supposedly instigated by political enemies, another sculptor did the present work, now near the Lima Art Museum, in which Candamo was represented standing in front of the presidential seat, "in vigilant attitude," according to Ascher junior.

While most monuments in Lima where inaugurated with pompous ceremonies normally attended by officials, diplomats and generals, one was inaugurated without anyone present. The monument to Mateo Paz Soldan, a Peruvian academic of the 19th century, was to be inaugurated by ex-President Augusto Leguia, but there was a coup by Gen. Luis Sanchez Cerro and the ceremony was forgotten until time, sun and humidity destroyed the rope that held a canvas and the monument became visible to all without any fanfare.

Lima, founded in 1535, is not the only Peruvian city where monuments do not necessarily correspond to reality. In Cusco, a city in the southeast of the country that was the centre of the Inca empire, a monument supposedly representing the chief Inca was modelled after a North American Indian warrior.
